title: An injection positioned past the last column is appended in ascending order by both entry points, not dropped and not left at its declared index
rationale: The branch enriched-stream-honours-injections-at-their-positions names in its own cannotCatch: 'injections at positions beyond the source length, where applyInjections has a separate append-in-ascending-order branch that no fixture reaches'. Making stream() honour injections reimplements exactly that branch as the merge's end-of-input drain, so the corpus should stop leaving it unreached. Position 99 against a three-column schema lands at column 4 on both entry points. The rule is surprising enough to be worth publishing - a caller could reasonably expect 99 to mean index 99, or to be rejected - and until now it existed only as a comment inside a private method.
catchesBugClass: The drain branch diverging between the two entry points, and the two plausible wrong implementations of it: one that drops the injection because the source is exhausted, and one that stamps the declared key rather than the next output slot, leaving a column at position 99 with a 95-column gap in front of it.
cannotCatch: It cannot see relative ORDER among several past-the-end injections - one is enough to reach the branch but not enough to show that the drain is ascending; the unit test consecutiveHeadInjectionsKeepTheirRelativeOrder covers ordering at the head, and the drain's ascending order rests on TreeMap.pollFirstEntry rather than on a fixture. It also cannot see that maxFields still counts source leaves only, so injections can push the output past a limit that names itself as a bound on the output.

predicted.detail: Both entry points emit the three source columns and then audit_tag as column 4.

configDescription: assert ENRICHED_KEYSET vs ENRICHED_STREAM, one injected field at position 99
